# TxID: Full Reference

> TxID is a white-label AI support agent that DeFi protocols and Web3 token projects embed on their site with a single script tag. It auto-detects the user's connected wallet, diagnoses failed on-chain transactions in plain English, answers questions from the protocol's documentation, and escalates to the human team when it cannot resolve something. Every answer is recorded with the conditions it was produced under, so it can be verified later. This file is the full, self-contained reference for answer engines.

Website: https://txid.support
Dashboard: https://app.txid.support
Contact: team@txid.support · Telegram https://t.me/Non_Fungible_Howard

---

## What TxID is

TxID replaces the manual, repetitive customer support that DeFi protocols and token projects run in Discord and Telegram. Instead of a human answering "why did my transaction fail?" or "where are my tokens?" for the thousandth time, an AI agent embedded on the protocol's own site answers instantly, grounded in that protocol's documentation and live on-chain data.

It is white-label: the agent uses the protocol's own colours, font, and logo, so it feels native to their site. A small "Powered by TxID" badge appears on the Evaluation tier and is removed on Enterprise.

## Who it is for

- DeFi protocols (DEXes, lending, staking, vesting, launchpads)
- Token projects and communities
- Any Web3 team fielding repetitive support questions about transactions, wallets, and how their protocol works

## Core capabilities

### Automatic wallet detection
When a user opens the agent, it silently reads the connected wallet address from whatever provider is connected to the site (MetaMask, WalletConnect, Coinbase Wallet on EVM chains, Petra or Martian on Aptos). Users who prefer not to connect anything can paste an address instead. It uses that address to look up balances and transactions on the relevant chain. No signing, no seed phrase, and no permission is ever requested. It reads public on-chain data only, so there is nothing it can do to move or access funds.

### Failed-transaction diagnostics
The agent replays a transaction and explains, in plain English, why it failed. It covers every common cause:

- **Out of gas**: the transaction hit the gas limit before the contract finished. This is about the gas limit set for the transaction, not the wallet's ETH balance; the fix is usually to raise the gas limit and resubmit.
- **Revert with a reason string**: a require() check failed and returned a human-readable message such as "insufficient allowance", "slippage", or "expired".
- **Custom errors**: modern contracts use gas-efficient custom errors (for example SlippageTooHigh()) that appear as a hex selector on a block explorer unless the contract's ABI is known; the agent decodes them using stored ABIs and a per-contract error glossary.
- **Solidity panics**: automatic compiler errors such as arithmetic overflow or underflow, division by zero, array index out of bounds, pop on an empty array, a failed assert, or out of memory.
- **Slippage or deadline exceeded**: the most common DEX swap failure. The price moved beyond the set tolerance, or the transaction sat past its deadline.
- **Insufficient balance or allowance**: not enough of the token or native coin, or a missing ERC-20 approval before a transfer.
- **Stuck or pending**: not a failure at all. The gas price was too low or there is a nonce gap; the fix is to speed up, cancel, or reset the nonce.
- **Move aborts (Aptos)**: Move does not have revert strings. An abort is a module address plus a numeric code, which means nothing on its own. The agent decodes it against the Aptos framework error tables and per-protocol error maps, and when a code is not mapped it says which module aborted and with what code rather than inventing a reason.

### On-chain lookups
For a connected wallet, the agent can fetch the wallet balance (native coin plus tokens), recent transaction history, open token approvals, a specific transaction's details, live contract state, and a watched contract's recent activity. Every lookup is on demand: the agent reads when a question needs it, and cites what it read.

### Sub accounts
Some protocols do not hold a user's funds in their wallet. A perps or margin venue gives each user a sub account, an on-chain object owned by their wallet, and that is where collateral and open positions actually live. Those users have two addresses. TxID resolves the sub account the moment a wallet connects and shows both, labelled, with the full address available to copy, so a trader never meets an unexplained second address and never has to trust a shortened one. Off by default, since most protocols have no such concept.

### The case record
Every answer is stored with the conditions it was produced under: the ledger version or block the answer was true as of, the prices any figure rested on, which tools ran and which lookups failed, the model, the response time, and a hash of the answer text. Records are append-only, enforced by the database rather than by application code, so an answer cannot be quietly rewritten after the fact. Access is logged, and a conversation can be exported with its evidence intact.

This is the part that separates "the bot said something" from "here is what the bot said, what it read, and when it was true".

### Documentation Q&A
The protocol pastes its docs URL in the dashboard; the system crawls and indexes it using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The agent answers questions grounded in that documentation, not hallucinated.

### Escalation
When the agent cannot resolve an issue, it opens a human support ticket for the protocol's team, capturing the conversation context, and delivers it to wherever that team already works: Slack, Discord, Telegram, Linear, GitHub or Jira. For the issue trackers, the created issue's URL is written back onto the ticket. A delivery that fails is retried on a backoff rather than lost, because a user who was promised a human and never hears from one is the worst failure a support product has.

### Channels
- **Embeddable web widget**: one script tag on the protocol's site.
- **Inline embed**: rendered inside a container rather than as a floating button.
- **React component**: `@txid/react` for direct integration.
- **Telegram bot**: the same knowledge base, running as a bot in the protocol's Telegram group.
- **REST API**: server to server, authenticated with the project's secret key.

## Supported blockchains

Live: Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Avalanche, Etherlink, and Aptos.

Aptos is Move-native rather than another EVM chain, so it is a separate integration rather than a config entry: TxID reads it through Aptos's own fullnode REST and Indexer GraphQL, resolves .apt names through the Aptos Name Service, and decodes Move aborts rather than Solidity reverts.

Solana, Stellar and TON are not live yet.

## How to install (three steps)

1. **Embed**: add one script tag before the closing body tag. Works with React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, or plain HTML. No SDK, no build step.
2. **Configure**: in the dashboard, set brand colours, paste the logo URL, add the docs link, and add smart contract addresses. The preview updates in real time.
3. **Go live**: publish. Most protocols are live in under five minutes.

## Pricing

- **Evaluation**: 150 conversations per month to prove TxID on your own protocol. Includes wallet detection, transaction diagnostics, documentation Q&A, custom branding, and the analytics dashboard. A conversation starts when a user opens the agent and sends a message, and ends after 30 minutes of inactivity; all messages in one session count as a single conversation.
- **Enterprise**: for protocols running the agent in production, priced to the platform. Higher volume, every supported chain, escalation integrations, the full case record with export, and priority support. Contact the team for a demo and pricing.

## Frequently asked questions

**What exactly is TxID?** An AI support agent you embed on your DeFi protocol or token project site. It reads the connected wallet, diagnoses failed transactions, answers questions from your docs, and escalates to your team, without the user leaving your site.

**How does wallet detection work?** It reads the public wallet address from the connected provider and uses it to look up public on-chain data. No signing or permission is required.

**What stack does it work with?** Any stack. One script tag; works with React, Next.js, Vue, Svelte, or plain HTML. No SDK, no build step.

**Which blockchains are supported?** Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, Optimism, Avalanche, Etherlink, and Aptos. Solana, Stellar and TON are not live yet.

**Does it support Aptos?** Yes, natively. Aptos is a Move VM chain rather than an EVM chain, so it is a separate integration: fullnode REST and Indexer GraphQL for reads, Move abort decoding instead of Solidity revert decoding, Petra and Martian for wallet connection, and Aptos Name Service for .apt names.

**Can I prove what the agent told a user?** Yes. Every answer carries the ledger version or block it was true as of, the prices any figure rested on, which lookups ran and which failed, the model, and a hash of the answer. Those records are append-only at the database level and can be exported.

**Can it explain why a transaction failed?** Yes. It replays the transaction and explains the cause in plain English: out of gas, revert reasons, custom errors, or Solidity panics.

**Is wallet detection safe?** Yes. It only reads public data and never asks the user to sign, share a seed phrase, or grant permissions.

**What counts as a conversation?** One session from the user's first message until 30 minutes of inactivity; follow-up messages in that session do not count separately.

**Is it white-label?** Yes. Evaluation includes custom colours, font, and logo; Enterprise adds a custom agent name and avatar and removes the "Powered by" badge.

**Where do escalations go?** Slack, Discord, Telegram, Linear, GitHub or Jira, whichever the team already uses. Failed deliveries are retried rather than dropped.
